entries.name: Conventional Commits and SemVer
entries.why: Release notes and version bumps derived from commit types.
entries.gap: Measured on 2026-11-25: 0 of the last 200 commits in any of the 11 repositories use the feat/fix vocabulary. The commits the system writes itself already have the header shape `<loop>: <description>` (watchdog:, queue:, lane:, deploy-ultrastable:), and the lint now holds every generator a workflow or script contains to it; 8 generator titles are on the shrink-only baseline because another program or record matches their text (Q-STD-conventional-commits). Titles written by people and code agents for a pull request lead with the rule or item id, which the queue and write-back loops key on, and stay that way: the public changelog is built from provenance rows, not from commit types. SemVer is in force where a version is a promise to a consumer (the HTTP and MCP contract_version, whose major is compared by standards --check); repository releases are not numbered because no package is published, tenants pin the core by commit hash and the seed's one tag is a calendar date.
entries.tracked_by: Q-STD-conventional-commits
entries.conformance: Every title a generator writes parses as `<type>[(scope)][!]: <description>`, the type being the loop. Requiring feat/fix on pull requests, or a SemVer release train, would produce types and numbers nothing reads; revisit when a package is published.
entries.cost: S (lint and five generator titles, done); S more for the eight baseline titles and their readers

entries.name: Open Policy Agent (Rego) policy-as-code
entries.why: Policy as code for standing rules and access decisions.
entries.reason: Evaluated for real. OPA is a Go binary or a WebAssembly bundle that the same binary must compile in CI; either way a third-party runtime enters the seed, which carries none. The policies here are already code and data with tests, evaluated where the decision is made: seed/autonomy/policy.json and seed/autonomy/default-policy-pack.json (limits and protected paths), the Worker's diff gate, and about a hundred `python3 -m foundation <rule> --check` rules in CI; request authorization uses OpenID AuthZEN (entry authzen). They are path globs, thresholds and file probes, not the cross-service authorization logic Rego is for. A Rego export of the policy files was weighed: nothing would evaluate it, so it would restate rules in a second language that could drift from the one that runs.
entries.revisit: When a customer requires their organisation's OPA to approve agent actions, or the same policy must be enforced outside Ultrastable's own code (another company's CI or gateway). The decision point is already one function per gate, so an OPA call can be added there.
entries.conformance: Full: Rego bundles evaluated by OPA (WASM in the Worker, binary in CI). Export: the policy files rendered as a Rego data bundle.
entries.cost: L for full adoption (new runtime in the seed); S for an export nothing reads

entries.name: AsyncAPI 3.0
entries.why: Describes message channels (queues, streams, webhooks) the way OpenAPI describes HTTP.
entries.reason: The only messages another party receives are outbound webhooks, and OpenAPI 3.1 (already generated) has a `webhooks` section for exactly that; the queues and D1 ledgers between loops are internal and are now described by their CloudEvents types. A second description document for one webhook channel would be a file with no reader.
entries.revisit: When a message broker or stream is offered to systems outside the org (a public queue, a websocket or an event stream).
entries.conformance: An asyncapi.json listing the webhook channel and the io.ultrastable.* event types.

entries.name: OpenTelemetry metrics, logs and traces (OTLP export)
entries.why: Telemetry any observability backend can ingest without an adapter.
entries.reason: Exporting needs somewhere to send it: an observability backend is a paid or third-party service with its own credential, and the rule is zero third-party runtime dependencies and nothing a person must mint. What exists is read by the system's own loops and public pages: tick_runs and the ledgers in D1 and ops/, the clocks in doctrine/clocks.json and /health. The naming half of the standard is adopted (row otel-genai: tool-call spans use the convention's attribute names behind a telemetry port).
entries.revisit: When an owner connects an observability backend (one /connect link). Cloudflare Workers can then export traces and logs over OTLP by configuration, and the telemetry port in seed/worker/src/agentic/core/ports.js takes an OTLP adapter with no change to callers.
entries.conformance: An OTLP exporter adapter and a configured destination.

entries.name: OpenSLO
entries.why: Service-level objectives as YAML that SLO tools evaluate against a metrics backend.
entries.reason: OpenSLO files are input for an SLO engine that queries a metrics backend; the system has neither (see row opentelemetry). Its objectives are already data that its own code evaluates on every tick: each loop's expected interval and stage deadline in doctrine/clocks.json, each queue priority's deadline in doctrine/balance.json, each goal's target in seed/autonomy/goals.json. Rewriting them as OpenSLO YAML would produce files nothing evaluates.
entries.revisit: When telemetry is exported to a backend that an OpenSLO-reading tool queries.
entries.conformance: An export of clocks, deadlines and goals as OpenSLO SLO objects.
entries.cost: S to export; the engine and backend it needs are the real cost

entries.name: Terraform / OpenTofu (infrastructure as code)
entries.why: One declarative description of infrastructure that works across cloud providers.
entries.reason: Evaluated for real. Running it needs three things the system is built not to have: a binary installed in CI (a third-party runtime in the deploy path), a state file kept somewhere and locked (a new store that, if lost or stale, blocks every deploy: a single point of failure), and a Cloudflare API token with account-wide rights stored where the workflow can read it. Today no such token exists: Actions prove who they are with OIDC and the site Worker, which holds the credential, performs the deploy. The declarative description already exists and is already reconciled by code on every merge: doctrine/topology.json lists every Worker, binding, route and store, validated by a JSON Schema, and deploy/deploy-workers.mjs makes the account match it and probes the result. A Terraform JSON export of topology.json was also weighed: it is about 60 lines to write, but nothing would run it, so it would be a file with no reader that could silently drift.
entries.revisit: When a second runtime provider ships (seed/ultrastable.json lists gcp-cloud-run, aws-lambda and self-hosted as later), or a customer must manage their system from their own Terraform. At that point emit Terraform JSON from topology.json as a generated, drift-checked file; full adoption (state and plan/apply in CI) only if the customer runs it on their side.
entries.conformance: Full: state backend, provider credential and plan/apply in CI replacing the deployer. Export: a generated main.tf.json from topology.json.
entries.cost: L for full adoption (and it adds a stored admin credential); S for the export
